We use these paint pens for our hobby of painting smooth river stones, and they are terrific.  The tips are firm and don't fray.  The only caution I would give is that you get the best and smoothest line if you 'pull' the pen toward you.  If you 'push' the line away from you (as you would if you're writing the letter "O"), you will get some feathering unless you ease up on the pressure.  Or, if you are drawing, just turn the stone so you are drawing the pen toward you rather than pushing it away from you.We have these pens in the Extra Fine point, the Fine point, and the Medium point, and we seldom use the tiny brushes anymore.  These pens allow us (and even our 92 year old Nana) to do fine detail work, and we love them!Note:  We always put a spray coat of sealer on our stones to protect the artwork.

Hello everyone! My name is Aspen, @Paraslider on Twitter, I'm an artist and animator entering college this year, and I'd like to say I've been using these for 2 years now and they still work fine to this day. Some problems arose with the paint itself, which I'll get into later.For now, I'll start off with a brief introduction to how these pens work. Posca pens are notable for their usage in graffiti and street art, so the pen nibs are pretty much made to go through the wringer. As long as the surface you're going on isn't *too* toothy, like a broken brick or something, you can expect the nib to last a while. That being said; if you plan to use these on any kind of paper, expect the paper to pill. Pilling is the result of the pen nib being so abrasive on the paper's surface that it rips up the paper's surface/tooth. It won't destroy the paper by any means if it's watercolor paper or heavier weight paper, but printer paper is never ideal for these. The way you activate these is fairly simple-- you just press the nib down on a surface a bunch until the paint fills the nib, alternating between shaking the pen (cap on, of course) and pumping the nib like crazy until you get a nice, clean, consistent stroke.Let it be known, though, you will be shaking these pens a lot. I don't want to understate this in the slightest. You will spend a lot of time shaking these pens. If your batch is particularly fussy, hours even. When I tell you I've spent upwards of an hour or two just shaking and pumping my pens for the second piece of art in particular, please believe me there. Once that's done, you should be smoothly sailing. If not, I can only refer you to Kasey Golden's posca pen videos on YouTube for troubleshooting and tips.For clarity, I'll describe the processes behind each of these art pieces, as the size you're working on and the surface material matters greatly.1- The first painting (the side profile of my OC, grey background) is something I was able to do with just this 15 pen set, and it was my first go with these, done around late 2018. Watercolor paper, 7x7 inch size if I remember correctly, and yes, the paper pilled here and there. It wasn't at all a distraction or a major flaw of the markers, and it turned out perfectly fine. It sort of feels like eraser shavings, and if you like the texture the pilling produces, feel free to keep it! if not, it's really easy to wipe off after the paint dries.As can be seen, with just the base 15 markers, a lot can be done. If you're looking for a challenge and can work in a limited color palette, this set can take you far. The colors dry opaque and are super vibrant as expected. The coverage, especially for 3M size, is really nice and it dries down smooth and matte, no streaks abound. Poscas are renowned for their ability to create flat, sleek color blocks, so if that's your thing, you'll love these.2- This next piece (pattern background, 4 characters) was a lot larger than the first one, and was done on a 16x20 inch canvas and it was completed around a month or two ago. It's clear that I expanded the color count here, and you can totally buy different colors of posca pens on amazon for relatively cheap if you get them in packs. Individual pens, however, tend to be a lot pricier and more of a hassle to get, like 6-10 bucks a pop. Unlike the paper, there was no pilling at all on a canvas surface and was overall a much smoother experience. It took a bit of getting used to the canvas's surface, but it was a really fun project regardless.Aside from all the troubleshooting I had to do.You see, herein lies my major point of contention with these paint pens, but I'm sure this isn't just limited to posca, but all paint pens in general. I was painting this on an angle, and the canvas was stationed on an easel. Because of gravity, you can expect some of your pens to go rogue on you. They may appear to dry out or get streaky, but this is just due to the orientation of your canvas. This can typically be fixed by pumping the nib and shaking, but I will admit even after a while of this, some pens just don't want to cooperate. Some might stay watery, and others might stay streaky, and some might just die on you, and that's when I suggest a replacement. For instance, the navy blue and regular blue colors here were really temperamental, but after some deep, mindful, therapeutic thoughts such as "goddamnit, please let me finish this before these die on me" I was able to power through. Don't give up on your pens because they're showing signs of wear, because there's a chance they might still work/can be revived.TL:DR; These pens are spectacular for any artist of any skill level, but they aren't perfect and have some flaws. The orientation of the pen and your canvas affects the flow of the paint. In general, you won't see these problems with a majority of your pens, but every once in a while this may occur to a few in your batch. These are lovely for color laydown and produce consistent vibrant hues. They are definitely an investment though, so consider how you intend to use them and if it's worth the cost. These will make a lovely gift for any artist or creative!

I haven't had any of the issues using these pens. first time getting them: You need to shake them, cap facing down for 3 minutes tops, and I mean a *real* shake. if you've ever had old acrylic paint in a bottle, and you had to shake them to stir it up, you know how much *umph* I'm talking about here. then you get a paper towel and fold it up, maybe even a piece of wax paper underneath if you worried about oozing pen paint everywhere, and you push the pen tip down on the dry towel. Hold it down for a good minute. This is the more laborious part because each pen tip may or may not be more dry/wet than the others. so it could seem like your pen is defective, but most likely you haven't put enough pressure on the tip for the paint to saturate the tip. I'd do circles or figure 8's so it doesn't feel like you're waiting for a proverbial elevator's worth of time for your pen to be functional. once the pen is saturated you'll all set, you might notice times where the tip will dry out, and you just dap it with the damp towel to fix that, if the paint is dried then a soft scrub with a damp towel may be needed. You might notice times where you start to get streaks, which means the pen needs a break. Cap it, shake it cap side down for a minute or so then you should be good to go. Now that the troubleshooting is over with here's my actual review.REVIEW:I bought these for multiple projects, rock painting, signing paintings, touching up miniatures, etc. these worked best on flat surfaces. those round mandala rocks that are everywhere didn't work well in my experience. after I got a sense of flow from the paint in the pen it was easier to write and color with it, but I didn't like the actual look on the pen since the paint is a matte finish. i was hoping for a glossier paint. the pigments in the paint are higher than anything else I own though, and I found myself just buying crystal clear gloss spray, and running out of paint in the pens before ever having a blowout and ink running out of my pens. I think that just has to do with individual pressure people put on their pens, it's a balance of firm enough like holding a screwdriver so it didn't shake when you use it, and remember there's a canister of paint in a pen, and slamming the tip down is just opening a socket for the paint, so using all your hand/arm power to press down would make the paint run free.So in conclusion, if you take the time needed these pens work great, they're made for drawing and painting on canvas or thicker "art" paper. That said rock art is doable just tricky sometimes, and coloring mugs or shoes could also be a viable use for these.

WOW! These are great acrylic paint markers! One of my favorite video acrylic painting teachers recommends these markers and uses them to sign her name on her painting at the end of each lesson. Another video teacher uses paint markers for projects that require a small line such as fine tree branches. I had purchased a couple of markers from a leading American acrylic paint brand and kept wondering why my markers didn't work like the ones in the video lessons. Then I saw this set and the price was so good I wanted to try them out. I LOVE these markers; the tips are actually as fine as advertised. The video instructor said she taped her caps on to be sure the markers wouldn't dry out.I think this set might be less expensive because the markers are smaller than the ones used in the videos. I don't think they are full sized Posca markers, but that is OK with me since it enabled me to get 12 beautiful colors. One full size marker of the American brand company cost about $7, while 12 markers in this pack was about $25 at the time I purchased them. I tried to find a volume on both brands of pen, but the Posca pen info is all in Japanese, and the American brand did not have a volume that I could find. I did find nib size--the Posca was 0.7mm and the American brand was 2.4mm. Both brands are about the same diameter, but the pens in this set are about an inch shorter than the other brand (Posca-4.75", other brand 5.5" with caps on).I tested the titanium white since some acrylic colors, such as yellow, are very transparent and need the area under them painted white first to give them good coverage. Both brands needed several coats of white to cover over a black line so I would say they were equal in transparency.I was concerned about the tips being firm enough to last a long time. I have a tendency to press too hard most of the time and some marker tips get mushy with use. Since the tip has to be pressed against a firm surface to prime with paint to get it flowing this could be a problem. I was pleased to see that the tips kept their point after pressing against the surface of my craft table (with a protective silicone cover over it).I needed a teal color but the set did not have teal. I pressed the tip several times to get a tiny puddle of a light blue and another puddle of yellow. I mixed a tiny bit of each color until I got a match close enough to what I needed, used a small paint brush to fill in where I needed to cover a mistake, and was very pleased with the result.I would highly recommend this set to any one wanting to try out acrylic markers. I don't know how long the markers will last since they are not full size, but I think if they are used carefully and capped immediately after use they will be OK. Tape placed around the cap edge of the marker to seal out any air leaks should help. The markers are a great size for adding to a travel crafts bag and would make great stocking stuffers for the painter/crafter in your family.

This is how every paint marker should be made. Instead of some compressed fabric point to carry/apply the paint, these have a hard plastic nib that the paint flows through. You still have to push down hard enough to compress point back up into the barrel to first get the paint to flow, but unlike every other brand, instead of partially dulling and rounding out the nib, you have a very fine point that you can use to either make precise lines and dots or go over an area more for wider effects. On top of that, when you go to use them again at a later date, they still work. Others almost always have dried paint in the point fibers so you have to work at getting the paint to flow once again and then, in addition to overly large lines, the paint flows unevenly because it's kind of flowing along the outside of dried up nib instead of through it.  Try these if you've almost given up on paint markers and if you have never used paint markers before, don't bother with any others. Hopefully, all the other brands will switch to this method.

First of all I must stress that these are PAINT markers and not Alcohol based markers. Both are good, but both behave slightly differently.This being said, these Posca markers are great. The color is bold, and really pops out on what you are using them on. However, these are NOT wide tips. They have a nice point to them and are not super fine. With the right angle, you can get a variety of thickness.Now, I've seen reviews that say that they pool out too much, and yes this can happen, but if you're careful you can prevent this from happening. This can also happen to other kinds of markers too. I started by slowly pressing the tip gently, and watched for the paint to start filling the nib. Once it stared I lifted the pen and waited for it to fill completely. The paint then smoothly flows out as you run it along the object you're drawing on. You may have to go over your line a few times to get a solid line, but with patience it'll look nice. Let the paint dry completely before going over it, otherwise the colors will bleed into each other. As I said, these paint markers are great. Colorful, bold, and works on many different surfaces. Just be careful and don't press down too hard, or the paint will pool out everywhere. I've included a test run of these on common scrap paper. No bleed through as long as you don't keep the pen on one spot for too long.

Of course, you have to shake them to mix the paint the same as you would a bottle of paint.A couple of times there was a bit of splatter but I’ve discovered that it doesn’t happen if you move the pen towards you.They are so easy to use and are perfect for doing detail work on rocks. I love these posca paint pens!  I mostly use them for painting on rocks, they are opaque and if you make a mistake it is easy to fix it by waiting till it is dry and then painting over the mistake.  If you are putting your rocks outside, they should have a clear spray coat applied, 4 or 5 coats.  First coat very light to seal the colors.  I found that if I didn't clear seal them with 4 or 5 coats, after a year of being out in the weather (very rainy here) the paint would flake off.  I'm waiting to see if more coats will prevent that, plus I clear coated both sides to be extra sure.  They haven't been through a winter yet.  I don't like the red color, it is too orangy for me, but all the other colors I'm happy with.  I also use them in my mixed media painting.  As long as I'm painting on a dry surface they seem to paint over anything without clogging.  If I'm very careful I can get a thin line made or tiny dots, or be more generous to fill in a larger space.  The construction of the tip is such that they can splatter tiny splats if you aren't careful, there is a bit of a learning curve to their use in detailed coloring.  But all in all, I'm very satisfied with these PC 1m pens.  I also have some in size 0.7mm in pastel colors that are wonderful and some sparkly ones.  Different tip on them.  They all work well.

I am a painter who does work in acrylic on canvas and I paint really detailed, *tiny* patterns. Getting that small with a brush, even the smallest ones on the market, is sometimes really difficult so I have been searching high and low for acrylic paint pens that work on canvas, work with traditional fluid/heavy body acrylics, and are fairly opaque. The Posca is one of the better brands I have found, especially at the price point. The paint is nicely opaque, it goes on canvas fairly easily, and there's a nice range of color.There's a few issues that make these less than perfect- the hard, nylon/plastic tips make the paint "splatter" if there's any texture at all on your canvas, and if you are painting over dried acrylic that's not perfectly smooth, that will happen. But it happens less than with the water-based Sharpies. The colors are a bit dull- they aren't rich, but they ARE opaque, so I find that I can just use the Poscas for the detail work (especially filling in tiny open areas) and then dab a little fluid acrylic over the center of what I did with the Posca and the color intensifies.All in all, these (along with the Derwent Graphik Painters) are the best acrylic paint pens for working on canvas that I have found. Definitely recommended.

We use these paint pens for our hobby of painting smooth river stones, and they are terrific.  The tips are firm and don't fray.  The only caution I would give is that you get the best and smoothest line if you 'pull' the pen toward you.  If you 'push' the line away from you (as you would if you're writing cursive and you are writing the letter "O"), you will get some feathering unless you ease up on the pressure.  Or, if you are drawing, just turn the stone so you are drawing the pen toward you rather than pushing it away from you.We have these pens in the Extra Fine point, the Fine point, and the Medium point, and we seldom use the tiny brushes anymore.  These pens allow us (and even our 92 year old Nana) to do fine detail work, and we love them!We allow our artwork to dry when we change colors, usually using a hair dryer to speed things along.  We also spray our stones with a clear coat spray, and these pens do not run.Tips:  When a pen is used for the first time, you'll need to "pump" the tip of the pen gently on a practice surface, like a paper plate or sheet of copy paper.  You will see the ink flow into the tip.  Then you'll need to cap the pen and shake it.  Draw a line on the practice surface, to make sure it is ready.  You will need to shake the pen every time you use it, and occasionally, you will need to pump it on the practice surface again, to get the ink flowing.  CAUTION:  If you depress the tip of the pen on your artwork, it will allow the ink to flow freely down the tip.  This will cause a "blob" on your artwork.

We've now purchased 2 brands of acrylic paint pens this summer... these (Posca, made in Japan) and Betem (made in China).  They've been a huge hit! It also creates an easy kids-adults interaction environment, which is helpful when they perhaps don’t already know each other well (as at a family reunion).  So all in all, great!!  Poscas were great in every way – they wrote on glass (we had some wine glass decorating going on – let the paint cure for a day or two), and the colors were vibrant.  They don’t have dual tips like Betem (meaning broad at one end, fine point at the other) but you can achieve fine, broad, or anything inbetween easily via pressure applied and angle of the pen.  The kids had no problem mastering that.  Betem had more colors and were considerably less expensive, but the Posca’s 12 colors were certainly sufficient – you just might have to wait your turn a little more for the color you wanted.  While both brands were a big hit, if you want to write on glass, get the Posca brand – Betem states they write on glass but our experience was that they absolutely do not.  Last comment -- these make for a good rainy day activity as well, but you might want to put down paper or such first.  We created acrylic paint spots and smears on a picnic table and deck, which isn't a big deal in that kid-oriented outside area, but it's a consideration for some locations.

While these are a little smaller than I had thought they were going to be, (chock that up to me not reading the description properly lol), these are actually a lot better than I was expecting.I've used paint pens before, albeit they were oil based paints by Sharpie, and I've got to say, I'm pleasantly surprised by Posca.I'd been leery of using them before because I'd heard they were notorious for gumming up and drying out but they don't seem to have that issue if you take care of them properly. Now I haven't used these extensively yet, but what I have done with them has been enjoyable thus far.Cons, the nibs are a teeny bit scratchy and if you're not careful with the paper you use or how much pressure you apply when drawing, the markers will "spit" so you'll get flecks of little paint everywhere. Likewise, sometimes they can "leak" in that while you're drawing you COULD end up with a blob in your line work, but I have deduced it's most likely caused by pushing the nib in accidentally while you move the pen. Additionally, dependant on the colour, they can take a while to dry so you'll want to give them time to do so between coats and or just use a heat gun or a hair dryer to speed up the process.Pros, a little goes a LONG way, so you don't really need to empty them in one go and they don't really need more than two coats, if that. They work on a multitude of surfaces like paper, plastic, metal, wood, vinyl, but as with most acrylic paints, you'll want to seal them for longevity later. One feature I thought was kind of cool is that they work with Copic makers~! You can use Copics on top of them, but you have to be careful not to use too much of the Copic ink in one spot or it might dissolve the paint. Lastly, these work surprisingly well with Shrink-Dinks~! Just don't use an excessive amount of the paint and be sure to coat them with varnish after so they stay.All in all, I'm glad I finally caved and bought these. Definitely recommend for people that want to give an acrylic paint pen a try~!

The Posca Markers I received were old and mostly dried out. I didn't return them because I needed them for a project, but their overall life expectancy is anticipated to be very low (if I didn't look up how to fix the issue), as the paint flow is pitiful and the nibs are brittle.The Fix - If you don't feel like reading, search on YouTube for "How To Refill or Recycle Posca Paint Pens." I took a pair of plyers and opened each marker by taking the cap off and screwing the top clockwise (in the opposite direction that you would expect to turn to open it), removing the clear plastic piece, and filling the marker with water. Once that was done I put the marker back together, screwed the top back on, put the cap on, and shook vigorously to break up and reconstitute the dried paint, and it worked!However, this was a long and messy process, and no one should have to pay money for an item they expect to work as advertised, and I didn't find this fix until after I finished my project. The amount of trust I have with Amazon and its sellers have dwindled to non-existent, not just with art supplies, but throughout all departments. Personally, I'm sticking with either ordering from Blick, or finding a 40% off coupon and heading to Michaels for now on because the two day shipping just isn't enough for me to want to put up with this crap anymore.

So I gave in and decided to try acrylic paint pens because I couldn't locate the huge plastic tub of brand new, never opened bottles of acrylic paint. The tub is somewhere in my craft studio, and that place is like a snake pit - I can't find anything! ANYway, I ordered three different sets of Posca Paint Pens - the 0.7 mm extra-fine pen tips and the 1.8/2.5mm medium bullet tip pens., as well as the black and white variety pack (sizes range from 0.7 to 8mm chisel tip to 15mm big mama jama).Takes a bit to get all the wrappers off. Then you need to 'burp' the tip (hold the pen with the tip pointing up, and with your thumb, press down to get rid of the air that's settled between the inner paint skin and the new felt/plastic tip inside where you can't see it). While burping is fun, this is tedious. And can leave you with bruised thumb tips. Yeah. It's a thing.Once they've been burped, the real non-fun part begins: you gotta prime them. You can shake, shake, shake senora, shake it all around, but you should have a piece of notebook paper or old foam core (I used foam core) so that once you've shaken the snot out of them, you can press down on the paper a few dozen times to coax the paint into the tip. Warning: you can and will poke through the foam core board with the fine tip pens, so be sure you're doing this on a surface that you don't care about - otherwise, it'll end up looking like it has the measles once you're done.You've probably read other reviews that say on certain pens you can pull the tips out and turn them around if they become frayed. I saw the same reviews. And I remember thinking, oh great - I'm gonna spend this kind of money on paint pens that aren't gonna last very long at all before I gotta swap the tips, and then have to get more pens sooner than later. Well, lemme tell ya, I've had these for over 2 months, with daily heavy use, and I've only got one tip that I should probably flip but haven't because I can still use it for larger coverage areas. So, don't freak out. They'll last a good long while.One bit of advice I learned was, don't push the pens away from you when drawing/filling/lining with them. The pens want to flow, and they will if you remember to pull them towards you, and pull them gently. Sure, rocks (in my case) have uneven surfaces and textures, but taking it a bit slower when it comes to outlining with a fine tip pen, you'll discover your pen doesn't skip or leave little eyelash-length splats or flecks.Another pointer is, if you're lettering with these pens and you make a mistake/paint blobs out, if you keep a few clean Q-tips/cotton swabs nearby, you can pop one into your mouth to get it a little moist, and swipe away the problem.The very cool thing about Posca Paint Pens is that, once they dry (and they dry very fast! bonus!) you can go right in with another color and have that color show up bright and clear. The pigment is thick and unless you're trying to make white stripes on a solid dark background, one coat will suffice.You *can* blend with the Poscas. Not very well, because they dry so fast. BUT! You CAN put enough paint down by allowing it to puddle/pool a bit with your first color, then come in with the second/lighter shade and swirl/blend to your desired shade. Don't worry if you get color on your pen tip. It'll come right off after a few squigglies on a scrap piece of paper. Do some curly-cues and once the other paint is visually off the tip, press down to get the pen's paint color to come back to the surface. Voila!Read around on other reviews to see how to get dried Posca Paint Pen residue off your clothes. It will come off finished furniture with a little elbow grease and WD-40; unfinished furniture, not so much. This stuff soaks right in and it's impossible to get out - so you might as well just paint the whole tabletop since you've already got your paint out!Hope this was helpful. The Poscas are expensive, but you're getting a high quality product. The writing on the pen's labels is minuscule and in Japanese, and while you're thinking hey, I can keep these in their cute little crayon type upright box, nah forget that noise. Just dump'em in a small plastic container, throw in a few Q-tips and maybe what's left of an old notebook you've had lying around, and then tote the whole thing to your favorite chair, break out the (clean) rocks and start painting!

I have been painting rocks. I bought some other brands of paint pens that leaked. Someone suggested I try Posca. These have been awesome. I love the coverage they give and no leaking. They are great for rock painting. So glad I spent the extra money to get the bigger pack.

I got these in the Fine Point size because I thought Extra Fine might be too small--I figure that I'd rather have a slightly larger tip to make filling larger areas less tedious and then go in with a small micron where finer details are needed. I use these in my sketchbook to add color to the pages, and I really love them! They don't bleed through the page, which is nice. They are vibrant, and the color selection in this set is great. Very versatile.I still think it would be nice to have a larger tip--I may buy some chisel tip or medium tipped pens in two or three colors that I know I'll use a lot.

I’ve used Posca pens on wood, vinyl, rocks, and paper. On wood, over a good primer coat of Zinnser, they held up extremely well. They were unfaded and didn’t peel or flake after a year of exposure to the elements, including heat, rain, and light sun exposure. (For comparison, bottled acrylic paint applied at the same time did fade.)They were also great and time-saving for adding details on a 3’ x 6’ painting.On medium-weight and up paper, they’re good.They stick great to cleaned rocks, but choose rocks that are as smooth as possible and work gently. I had a tiny bit of texture on my rock, and it made the tip of my pen fuzzy.On a soft leather-textured vinyl iPad cover, they stuck well and didn’t rub off. They could be scraped off, but I didn’t spray with a protectant.All the colors cover well. The white (as typical of almost all white paint) takes multiple passes to cover. The black is silky and opaque on the first pass.There are lower-priced paint pens, but Posca are still the best if you want professional-looking, long-lasting results.

I know these are usually a pretty expensive product, but let me tell you that it is truly worth the money. I use these EVERY single day for my artwork, even if only for one or two details. Perfect for anything and everything I need. I flows well with most other types of media. I will always use POSCA!

Content:
I used to experiment with lots of different types of art mediums in the past and one of them were acrylics markers. It was fun and easy to use since I am more familiar with pens when it comes to drawing. However, the old markers I had purchased wouldn't always fill in the area I colored, and sometimes rubbed off the previous layer.

Fast forward to today. I have seen lots of instagramers playing with posca pens and they piqued my interest, but not enough to begin to even invest in them. I kept remembering my past experiences and I remember more cons than pros to them so I strayed far away from them thinking it was not worth the investment. My friend happened to buy some posca pens because of the hype. I saw her drawings in real life and found it so shocking. The pens, even though they were extra fine, did not leave any scratches nor did the nibs rub off. It really made me want to try them so I thought, why the heck not. If I didn't like them then I could give it to my nieces to play with. I am soooooo glad I finally gave these pens a try after sooooo much time eyeing them. Everything I felt peeved about my old acrylic markers have been solved with this brand and I couldn't be any happier. I started using them on grided notebook paper so that it would be more obvious that I was using the posca pens then just some ordinary marker (like copics or something). I especially love them because they have a limited color range. I was a lil skeptical about it at first but definitely appreciate it now. I always use the same colors over and over again with other mediums so my artworks would always look the same, but since posca pens only have a few colors (or at least the ones I bought) it pushed me out of my comfort zone and choose colors that I would normally never put together into a piece, and as a result, actually liking it (rare for me to like my own drawings). So yes, I do really think they are worth the purchase.

P.S I also like to draw Link from Legend of Zelda a LOT.

I have been looking at Posca Paint Markers for a long time and finally purchased the 21 Extra Fine (1mm) and the 29 Medium (5mm) Tip sets. I use them on Polymer Clay pieces. The variety of colors is a real plus. The paint does adhere to the clay very well. The outer part of the marker is made of a sturdy plastic material, which feels very solid and is comfortable to hold. The one thing I wasn’t expecting was the need to go over the colored areas several times to get a solid, opaque covering. Once I baked the clay with the colors on the surface, the colors remained vivid and bright coming out of the oven. I did use UV resin to seal the colors and protect them. There are so many things I can use these paint markers for to embellish the pieces I make. The Markers are easy to get started and use. I am very pleased with them and will continue to have fun using them on my polymer clay pieces- they’re great!! The one thing that prevented me from buying these markers in the past is the price. I really do think they are too expensive and the price needs to be reduced. Hence the 4 Stars. Yes, I finally did get an opaque finish but it took multiple applications (4-5 coats) to get there. If it took just one or two coats, I wouldn’t be so concerned about the cost.

Guys these pens are amazing! I'm an artist who hates to paint. I know that's a contradiction, but it's true. I love to draw though! I was struggling to get some paintings finished (I got bored with them) when I thought I'd try paint pens - a combination of painting and drawing, right? With crossed fingers I bought these after doing some research. I already had a couple of random paint pens from 'the other guys' I'd used to sketch with and lay down outlines, but they weren't amazing and they were hard to use. However when I tried the Tooli pens I was really impressed! First of all the tips (I got all Xtra Fine) are very nice, firm, pointy, can get good detail. Very responsive. Love that they send extras! Note that if you puddle two different colors together they will instantly combine, kind of like water colors. Be prepared for that quick bleed. I recommend these to artists who want to doodle on canvas; works great!!

**I use these for rock painting so I can't speak to how they behave on canvas/paper. But results are probably similar**

You really do have to shake these up A LOT to get the true color and when you finally get it flowing you have to constantly stop what you are doing and pump the tip get it to flow again... the tip just dries too fast. Speaking of the tip... it's plastic (which is probably why the paint dries on it so quickly). And if you have to layer colors, no matter how careful you are or how dry the paint is, the tip scratches up the first layer. They also spit/splatter while using... even on my smoothest santorini stones...ruining your art in many cases. And some colors take much longer to dry than others and compared to other brands.

I love to color and I bought these acrylic paint markers to add fine detail to my work. I saw them talked about on TikTok and decided to give them a try. The assortment in colors is nice, but only after having them for a month they are all dried out. I'm not sure if I received a bad batch or what. They are extremely difficult to shake up, and are a pain to get the color down from the tube and into the brush.

I am not sure if I was supposed to store these markers horizontally and not vertically? But storing them horizontally is not always practical for me. I'm thinking maybe by storing them vertically, this allowed for the paint to gather in the bottom of the pen and harden which resulted in them drying out.

When they did work, they had a really nice color and performed well. They allowed for fine detail when I colored. After shaking the pen for what seemed like 5 minutes (and the paint finally got flowing), it didn't write streaky and was well-pigmented. However, I don't think I will be buying these again.

I use them primarily on smooth wood that is coated with black chalkboard paint but I have also used them on cardboard, paper, canvas, and plastic. Have never had any issues with chipping after drying (I do not use sealant). Signs stay pretty dry, so I can't speak to how the acrylic handles an accidental splash of liquid.

The fine detail nibs are incredible and aren't easily ruined or dulled. Distribution of paint is consistent, though when it gets low you may find yourself pressing the tip more often. Nibs are easily replaceable and washable if you hit a clog (proper storage is necessary).

The colors in the E+ pack are perfect for what I need as a sign artist and you really can't beat the price for what you get. 5/5 stars by far.

I paint rocks...

I‘ve developed a love/hate relationship with these pens. They can be great or awful depending on the surface you’re working on

The colors are fantastic and the pigment density/coverage can be very good. They take a little longer to shake/mix the other pens. If not shaken long enough the pigment doesn’t mix with its base and you’ll get a weird syrupy liquid that’s not true to its color. It usually winds up being much darker than it should be. This can create problems with inconsistencies and color that doesn’t match. So shake, shake shake and have a piece of paper handy to dab, dab dab! You’ll need to “milk” the pen to bleed off any unmixed color that collects at the nib.

The paint is shiny which I didn’t expect & might be helpful for shoppers to know. When working on a hard, non porous surface the first coat of paint will dry quickly and peel as you’re still applying color. This leads to a terrible surface texture as little bits of paint flakes pull up and mix in leaving a lumpy, bumpy, ugly designs. I was ready to toss these in the garbage til I tried them on a new type of rock I purchased...then everything changed!! On the slightly more porous rocks they were incredible!! None of the same issues existed. They created an even, densely colored coat with no flaking issues!

There’s one aspect to these pens that are superior to poscas. The nibs are harder (and maybe even smaller?) and the paint consistency slight different so you can get really thin lines and so some very precise work

It might be wise to get a smaller set of these if available to try them first and see how they do on the surface you’re planning to work with. If it’s a match then you’ll really enjoy these pens and the colors offered

I’ve attached a picture of a few of the rocks I’ve made. I mix media so keep in mind that not all the colors seen here are from the markers

UPDATE: I’ve come back to update my review after working with these pens for a good length of time. I’m loving them! I never even use my expensive Posca pens anymore. The density of color and range of colors is fantastic! The “texture” of the paint is beautiful to work with. The only draw back is the shaking/mixing of the pens. It is difficult to mix them well....it takes a good bit of shaking and “milking” before you start to paint. It’s a small gripe but it’d be easier if they mixed quicker and more thoroughly.

Originally I didn’t like the sheen of these pens since I was used to the Poscas but now I’ve come to hate the Poscas chalky finish which can create an uneven surface and clumps and looks dull in comparison. These pens make a nice even fluid coat

I’ve added a few more pictures of my newer pieces. I love what these pens can do!

Our family has had a generally positive experience with the Funcils 5 Acrylic Black Paint Pen set. These versatile pens have proven to be quite useful for a variety of creative projects that we engage in together. The assortment of tip sizes – ranging from 1mm to 15mm – has allowed us to explore different techniques on a variety of surfaces, including plastic, canvas, wood, and even glass.The fine tip options were particularly handy for intricate detailing, while the jumbo pens were perfect for broader strokes and bolder designs. This variety made the set a go-to tool for family crafting sessions, where each of us could find the right pen for our respective projects.The ink quality is generally good, providing rich and consistent coverage across different surfaces. However, we did notice one minor drawback that led to a 4-star rating. The issue revolves around the ink flow control. It appears that there can be an excess of ink on the nib when starting to use the pen, which can result in a messy application if not carefully managed. We found that pressing down the nib to help the ink flow actually caused the opposite problem – an overflow of ink that quickly made our designs messy.This isn't a dealbreaker for us, as we've learned to delicately control the flow by wiping the nib before use. It's a small inconvenience, but it's worth mentioning for those who might be new to using paint pens. Once we got the hang of managing the ink flow, the pens performed admirably and allowed us to bring our creative visions to life.All in all, the Funcils 5 Acrylic Black Paint Pen set has earned its place in our family's creative toolkit. The range of tip sizes and the ability to work on various surfaces make it a versatile choice for our crafty endeavors. While the issue of ink flow control does exist, it's manageable with a little practice, and the results are definitely worth the effort. If you're looking for a set of paint pens to spark your family's artistic side, this one is definitely worth considering.

I was lucky enough to be able to test three different Funcils sets at the same time (gold, silver, and black).  Many acrylic pens require constant shaking to maintain paint flow, but these have no such issues.  They take some time to prime but, once that’s done, the paint flows very smoothly.  If anything, it may be a little too fluid for some tasks.  It’s runnier than others I’ve used and a lot can come out at once, which means longer drying times (10+ minutes in some cases).Once fully dry, it has a nice semi-gloss finish that feels very durable.  The drying characteristics often depend on the material you’re drawing on, however.  I found these worked well on watercolour paper and canvas but, when used on smooth surfaces like plastic or glass, they have a tendency to rub off.  I think they’re best suited to porous materials like fabric, canvas, wood, or stone.The different Funcils colours generally mark well on each other (please see photo...and try not to notice that I managed to write one entire section upside down).  The silver and gold stand out nicely on the black (and vice versa), but I found they don’t cover over darker colours quite so well.  They’re often streaky and need at least two coats to achieve a good opaque layer.  The semi-gloss finish might also make it harder for other paints to adhere, so these may not be the best choice for a base layer.I really liked the variety of different nibs.  The fine nibs (1 and 3 mm) are great for detail work, but the markers are so similar in size/shape that I often grab one thinking it's the other.  The 3 and 6 mm nibs are reversible (bullet and chisel tips), and the 15 mm nib has a unique flattened chisel tip with three flat surfaces.The only major concern I have is longevity.  They don’t seem prone to drying out, but I’ve only been using them for three days, so it’s hard to reach a full conclusion in that time frame.  I also worry that, since they tend to put a lot of paint out at once, they’ll run out faster than other pens.  Only time will tell in either regard.At $15.95, I think these are well-priced for the quality and variety they offer.  Most comparable sets only have one or two pen sizes, but these are well-suited to a range of applications.  The paint itself has a couple of minor issues but, from what I’ve seen so far, I’d certainly recommend them.My rating: 4.5 stars

We love paint markers in this house!  I have a lot of grandkids, and when they come over, they almost always want to do a craft project.  As you might imagine, paint markers can come in very handy for crafting.  This set of 24 markers is very nice.  I tried out the colors using both the ball-tip and paintbrush tip.  The color feeds beautifully, without any kind of priming, which is often a feature of paint markers.  I love the pretty, vibrant colors, though I do agree that a true red, and a true kelly green would be nice.  But for most purposes, the slightly off-colored green and red are just fine.  None of the grandkids have mentioned this at all, so I'm definitely quibbling.  The markers came in a flimsy cardboard box, without any kind of separation.  So if you've pulled a number of the markers out of the box at the same time, chances are excellent that the rest of them will just fall down on their sides, requiring you to shake them out of the box.  To save myself the hassle, I found a conveniently-sized plastic storage container (the disposable ones you can get at the grocery store, or dollar store), and the markers are all now happily living in there.  I like that it has a cover, too.  You do need to be careful to close the caps firmly on the markers (just like all markers), so your paint doesn't dry up.  Time will tell how durable these markers are; but at $14.99 for 24 markers (as of this writing), I won't feel badly about just replacing them when the time comes.

I used these acrylic pens to paint rocks. It was my first time painting rocks so I was unsure what products to buy. I first used acrylic paint and brushes for the background on my rocks. I can have a shaky hand and inconsistent handwriting on paper but I think most of the handwriting came out pretty good on the rocks. Every once in awhile, if the rocks had a little dip or crack or something in it, the marker would catch and mess up my writing. I'd just paint over it and wait for it to dry then try again. Luckily this didn't happen very often. Think that's more of a rock painting issue though, not a problem with the product. When writing, I learned to write very slowly. If you go to fast the tip will sling paint. If you go slow, you'll have a much better result. I did notice sometimes the pens would appear to dry out as others noted in reviews, but with a few shakes or some pressure on the tip, I've been able to get the pens to start working perfectly again in no time. I've painted over 100 rocks (some a few times - when i didn't like something about my first try 😅) and all of the pens are still fully functioning and seem to have plenty of paint left. The white pen, which is one of the ones I've used the most, has started to crack a little on the tip (see picture). I think it may just be because I'm writing on uneven rocks though. If I don't pay attention, the cracked tip makes the handwriting very bad as it causes the paint to come out inconsistently. I just make sure to tilt the white pen a certain angle and it works just as it did when I first bought it. I do wish the pens differentiated between the finer and medium point tips. I threw them all in one box and the pens have no markings to indicate if they're fine point or not. Luckily, both tips seem to work fine for what I'm using them for. There's not a huge difference between the two but it would be nice to know. Overall, great pens. Definitely recommend!

I call these "generic Chinese pens" because the box and pens don't have a company/brand name on them, and I've seen the same set for sale on Amazon under at least 2 different company names. If you're going to buy them search Amazon and buy the least expensive - you'll know they're the same because of the box design and the lettering on the pens.  The quality is pretty average for this type of pen.The instructions on the included 'instruction manual' say to shake them at least 30 times before using and I found out why - if you don't mix them thoroughly before each use you can end up with watery thin paint, or tiny clumps of paint. The description calls them 'extra-fine' - I'd  call it medium fine but they do make good lines.  In my opinion the color selection is just OK - I'd like to have a brighter green and blue than these. I did a swatch chart so you can judge for yourself, but note the colors are not numbered or named on the pens or caps, and the cap color is only a general indication of the paint color.  I couldn't get the colors to blend well either when they were both wet, or by overlaying one color on another dry color.  The colors do show up pretty well on black paper which is a plus to me (see the doodle I uploaded). On the down side these seem to be very wet paints even when thoroughly mixed and they do bleed through thin paper.  I haven't used them on rocks, plastic or ceramics but I suspect they would be better suited for those materials.  If you do use paper you'll probably want to use a heavier weight (like for watercolors or mixed media).  Because of the wetness they take a bit longer to dry than other acrylic pens I've used.Important: You'll need to prime these after mixing before the first use - quickly press the tip straight down on some scrap material and release - you'll see the nib (tip) fill with paint.  I'd recommend using cardboard as there's a good chance of ending up with a puddle or drips.  Also I'd recommend doing a line on scrap paper before actually using to remove any excess paint from the nib.  The instructions say if one gets clogged you can remove the nib and wash it out with warm water, but I'm not going to try that as it would undoubtedly make a mess.  I have yet to use these where I didn't end up with a little paint on my hand.  As far as storage, the box isn't going to last long - if you do buy these I'd recommend keeping them in a cheap pencil case (there are plenty on Amazon).  All in all these are OK pens for casual use at the current price, but if you want professional quality definitely look elsewhere.

I've never used Posca markers before, but having recently entered the adult coloring community, I have heard others sing their praises, and now I can say, rightfully so.  This "holiday" set of 22 markers is really 11 makers of the 3 m and 5 M variety.  Same colors - just different sizes.  The colors include:  black (a beautiful opaque black) and white (equally gorgeous for a paint marker), pink, lavender, light pink, blue, orange, sunshine yellow, light green, aqua green, and sky blue.  I'm not sure why this termed a holiday set.  It is coming out near Christmas and yet the set does not contain what you might consider a traditional Christmas red or green.  (Actually, if you get the larger 62 count set, I bet there is one in it. )  It also does not have any "holiday" packaging aside the very nice hard side (?) case that the markers come in which I suppose makes it giftable. The color is bright and yet opaque.  I just wrote some words with the colors on marker paper and was extremely surprised by the quality.However, my one "concern" is that the markers themselves feel rather light, which makes me wonder exactly how much paint/ink is in them and how long I can expect them to last before I need to replace them.  Posca markers not cheap.  They are at the highest end of paint makers in the field.  Please see the 62 ct set in this listing if you are unsure of what that means.  I guess I just want to know that I'm getting my money's worth at the price point.  I also think that I would have preferred to have this set with more colors at the same size for the price rather repeating the 11 colors just to have two different sizes.  But overall, this is a quality set.  NOW I GET IT.

I use markers for a variety of crafts, and have purchased way too many glitter, metallic and other specialty markers online and from local craft stores.

WHAT MAKES THIS A GOOD SET:
First, that you get so many different styles of markers in one big box that's easy to store. Anyone that has priced buying these in small sets or even individually will appreciate that.
The glitter pens are pretty glittery. I have a few glitter pens that are a different brand that are more glittery, but they were expensive pens that I had to buy individually from a local craft store. For the price of these, the glitter effect is pretty good.
The metallic markers are also pretty good. The effect is comparable to other brands I have that cost slightly more than these.
You get a good variety of colors in the Classic, Pastel, Neon, Morandi (which are "muted" colors btw, vs bright neon colors). The white, and other light-colored markers do a great job - bright and easy to see on dark paper.

THINGS TO KEEP IN MIND:
When you want to use one of these markers, you kinda have to "get them flowing" initially. They printed a little diagram on the side showing you how to pump them to get them flowing. If you're not getting a very strong, bold line, you need to pump the marker some more, to get the ink flowing better.
Due to the nature of how ink flows from these markers, you can get the best result using them if you're very purposeful in your marks. If you want to make quick, very fast marks, these may not be the pens for you.

- My biggest complaint is the box they come in. The way that this box is depicted in the product description pictures makes it seem like it arrives in a tiered, organized box. It's just a box. It's a nice box, but it's just a box, without any tiers or dividers. The markers themselves are numbered, and the back of the box has a chart or "key" that you can use, to identify what type of marker each number is.
Additionally, the names of the actual colors are not on the box, nor are they on the markers themselves. This might not bother you, but for colorblind folks like myself, not having the actual name of the color written on these markers can be a bit of an issue.

Overall, this is a good variety of specialty markers that I'm sure to get a lot of use out of.

First time using paint pens of any kind, so take this review with a grain of salt ofc!!

Was apprehensive about buying something like Posca pens because of the price and not knowing whether or not I’d actually enjoy them, so I decided to try these as like a…trial run I guess.

PROS:

Firstly, they are super easy to use. I particularly like the brush nib because it allows for that line variation and filling in larger areas.
Something to note is that I’m using suuuuuper thin (A5) paper, and so far, after layer upon layer—the paper hasn’t buckled hardly at all!! Was a really nice surprise tbh!! In fact, the only thing that made it buckle and bleed through was the pen I was using for my lines after laying down the paint. I have been having so much fun experimenting with the colors (which there are a lot!!)

CONS:

Be prepared to layer these. They aren’t suuuuper duper pigmented like others I’ve seen especially if you’re laying a light color over a dark one, even after shaking them for a bit as it says to do on the back of the box. (Though in all honesty, I enjoy it more as a feature than a con, but I know some people might not find that appealing—but it could be that I’m impatient and don’t shake them long enough before use)
Something I also noticed is that there are NO lighter/pastel type colors. It’s not a huge deal, but I’d really love a few of those just to lighten things up if I need to. Generally good flow, but some of the markers have little fibers on the nib that need to be picked off. ALSO. Before you start layering, give the first layer a little bit of time to dry. I noticed it takes about 10 seconds but then you’re good to go!!

I will say though, for the price and what you get, they work wonderfully and other than what I listed above I can’t think of any complaints!! Great for anyone like me who hasn’t tried them before and doesn’t wanna break the bank on other brands. :)

This is a good paint marker set to have on hand for creative moods. 80 colors, and they're well arranged in a way that you can get some really nice tonal variations to make your work pop. The tips are medium felt bullets and they have a durable feel with a medium amount of give. 6I like the medium bullet tips but they're a little on the large side for fine detail work, but I won't complain about that. I'm still very satisfied with the sheer quantity of luxury acrylic markers you get in this set.  The organizer is made of a durable, water-resistant nylon material and the pages are sewn of the same material. The zipper on the case is extremely well made and is also durable. This case is fitted with a carrying strap. Very good case should definitely outlast the markers and is REUSABLE.My opinion of the marker puts them high up on my charts as a well made and highly usable artist's toolI particularly like the variations of color in the set. The quality is appropriate and even though you could probably find better markers, I don't think you're going to find a set of this value.I definitely suggest this item to anyone, and I think it would make an excellent gift idea.

This set of 80 acrylic paint pens earns a mixed review.  The pens are neatly packaged in a sturdy and organized zipper case.  This makes storing the pens horizontally easy and ensures your art area is not messy.  I laid out the case and took a piece of pre-cut 4X6-inch white cardstock.  I attempted to start drawing with the black pen.  I couldn’t get the cap off the paint pen.  I eventually had to get a rubber gripper that is used to remove jar lids.  I got into a rhythm and was soon able to remove the tops off the sample pens I tried as I drew my drawing.  I needed to twist and pull using the rubber gripping pad.  If you have arthritis, you may have to work around the fact that the tops are incredibly difficult to get off the paint pens.I started with the black pen, creating a basic drawing to fill in with different colors.  First, I used traditional paint markers to fill in the petals of the flowers.  Then, I used several metallic markers to fill in the flower center and leaves.  Finally, I touched up the black ink and attempted to do some detail work.  I colored the four blue corners last.  The three white dots in those corners took three coats with the white acrylic paint marker.  In contrast, the whitish/grey coloring on the stems is one coat with the white marker (see photograph).The paint pens dry fairly quickly.  I got several paint spots on my hands, which I cleaned with a scrub brush, warm water, and hand soap.  The black pen easily covered minimal mistakes made while coloring the petals and center.  I had to use a light touch, or the nib would wear away my paper. I used a metallic pen to color the center of the flowers. The paint flow was too heavy and made a mess when I opened it.  Eventually, that particular marker’s paint flow slowed, and I could continue to use it.I decided to test whether these paint pens are waterproof and quick-drying.  I waited fifteen minutes after I was done with the drawing.  I wetted down a paper towel with three squirts of water and dragged it two times across the right-hand side of the drawing.  The ink did not smear on the paper but lifted off and covered my paper towel (see photograph).  I have concerns about using these paint pens on anything exposed to water.  Paint from both the regular and metallic pens was present on the paper towel.On another 4X6-inch piece of cardstock, I used two colors to write letters, numbers, and common words  (see photograph).  As you can see, the medium-sized nibs make detailed drawing and writing difficult.  The manufacturer does not hide this; few examples of tiny writing or detailing are on the product description page.  Additional acrylic pens to finish your artwork may be necessary, depending on what you are creating.This paint pen set is much better than others I have tried, but it misses the mark with caps that can’t be easily removed and paint that is not waterproof.  Even with that in mind, I believe this is still a good value for 80-paint pens.  This set may work for you if you are a doodler and want to have fun.  However, if you are serious about your art, you may need to look elsewhere to be completely satisfied.

Absolutely love these. I originally bought the 72ct. After a couple months I decided I liked them well enough to buy the 130ct. For a larger variety.
(First pic is of the 2 sets side by side without the opposite sides of the fold out sections.)

There’s a couple differences between the 2 sets outside of the obvious color range. The 72ct came with just the markers in the case. I expected the same from the 130ct however I was pleasantly surprised to find a baggy of replacement nibs and instructions on how to replace said nibs as well as instructions on how to fix them if they become dried out.

Pros:
- Easy control
- Smooth consistency and flow.
- Juicy
- Bright, bold, vibrant, gorgeous colors.
- If your main qualifier is brush tips these are perfect! Capable of creating thick lines but also capable of creating those fine details as well as get into the smaller nooks and crannies.
- layer well with like colors.
- No smudging or smearing.
- Dry quickly
- Fine tip is great for dotting. I’ve used them primarily for adding dots and other embellishments over top blocks of color.
- Case is well made and makes for easy storage as well as taking them on the go.
- good color variety in both sets making smooth and subtle color transitions a breeze.
- NO BLEEDING

Cons:
- 3 of the markers in the 72ct arrived dry, however not entirely. (Upon receiving instructions in the larger set in how to fix this I feel this has been made up, tho these instructions should be included in the smaller sets.)
- The fine point is not very fine, it is indeed a small bullet tip that doesn’t do well at all for fine details. The brush tip works better.
- There is some color consistency issues between the brush and bullet tip on some colors however slight.
- Some of the fine tips leave behind fibers.
- These do NOT work well on fabrics, colors will not show.
- Majority of the colors do not appear well on black surfaces. (This does not seem to be the case coloring over lines in coloring books).
- Not all colors layer nicely as these are water based, if you attempt to layer colors on opposite sides of the spectrum they just mix.
- There is only one Red in the 72ct.
- Some colors are more transparent than opaque in the fine tip.

Overall, very worth it. I have sets Ive paid more for that were far less quality.

No issues with snapping or breaking at all.I still have nitpicks about the color range (lack of oranges and yellows, mostly) but have found that, while they're still wet, they do mix quite nicely. You can achieve a lot of good in-between colors by mixing on the surface you're creating on before the marks dry.Though I am still so sure I will run out of white and yellow before anything else, which has me wishing I could buy individuals.Despite that, these are one of my favorite sets of art supplies in recent years. I'm obsessed.Updated pros/consPROS:-Surprisingly opaque-very saturated colors-dries fast and layers well (colors do dry a bit darker, as it goes with acrylic)-The brush tip is actually the best, no more pumping a paint markerCONS:-color range is lacking a bit in oranges, yellows, and dark colors-case takes up a lot of space when opened--------------------------------original review--------------------------------(I got these today, so this is a 'first impressions' review)I'm a artist and art instructor by trade, and I like to use a wide variety of materials to make recommendations to students as well as find new supplies for myself.These markers are pretty solid- I like acrylic paint for its opaque layering properties, as well as the quick dry, and these markers are pretty effective at both. As with acrylic paint, you do have some transparency and a need to layer, especially on lighter colors like white and yellow, or on top of darker colors. But overall, the coverage is pretty solid and the saturation is impressive.The case is a bit weird, you have to be careful separating the layers (they tuck into these little ridges at the back to hold together, and I can see there being a risk of snapping) but otherwise it seems convenient.The color range is odd. Acrylic dries darker than it applies, so after you let them sit for a moment you do have deeper hues, but the black included is SO much darker than the deepest of any other color.I'd really love to see a deep jewel tone range for each hue so I can achieve solid depth without just resorting to black. A deep alizarin crimson, phthalo blue or Paynes grey, deep viridian- the problem, I assume, is that these markers all have an almost chalky binder to keep the opacity up, and it sacrifices the deeper values as a result (many of the above listed colors are traditionally transparent.) So I'm not sure this would even be possible with the current pigment/binders used.Still, it would be wonderful to have a really deep set of colors, and if I'm just missing them in this 60 pack, I'd love to be directed to where I can grab them.Also, there's not a lot of orange options, and there are a whole lot of certain other colors, like green and pink.Anyway tldr;PROS:-nice opacity-very Saturated-dries fast and layers well-smooth flow with convenient brush tipCONS:-color range is lacking in oranges, yellows, and dark colors-case is a bit confusingI'll come back after a couple months of use to update on whether the markers have any trouble or not, but as of today I'm liking them.

The box that these come in is really nice. It's hard plastic, with each tray coming out separately. You can take out one tray, then put the top on that so you have a handle to carry it, so you don't have to take the entire box with you if you don't want to. It's also compact, so it won't take up much room, and the markers can lay horizontally, which is the way acrylic markers should be stored.  I found this box to be the very best feature of the set. I swatched the colors on the swatch sheets that came with it (one white and one black) and I wasn't terribly impressed. The pens are ok, but one application didn't cover the black line around the swatch box on the white card, and on the black they were fairly streaky. I realize that paper isn't the best medium for using acrylic markers (canvas paper, glass and metal would be much better) but I expected the paint to have a little better coverage. I do like that they hold a lot of paint, and that each marker has a number that corresponds with the swatch sheet. I also like the window in the marker that shows how much paint is left, and I really like the brush nib as opposed to hard nibs some other markers have.Do I think this set is worth $69.99?  No. I have other acrylic markers that perform as well, although they might not hold as much paint, and don't have the awesome box. But I'm cheap, so you be the judge.

I have been collecting a few sets of acrylic marker/paint pents so that I could do some detail work on paintings, models, or artwork and not have to use a brush for some things.

HOW THIS COMES
This comes in a great case. It has a lot of room in it and is very well laid out. They are easy to see and use from a chair or table.

MARKERS
The markers themselves are brush on one end and fine point on the other. There is no window on the side to see the paint level and you do not have to shake them to get them to work.

COLORS
This set has a LOT of colors. If you do anything like rock painting or other bright colored projects, you will have plenty to choose from. Some of the colors are similar, but I don't mind because if one runs out or dries up, I can just change to another.

PERFORMANCE
On paper, these are pretty good intensity. They are not as opaque or thick as some others I have but they still work great for projects that don't need a heavy opaque laydown of paint. On canvas, they are hit and miss. Some of the colors are more transparent than others and will need more coats. The best ones on canvas are the metallics as they cover well and the texture is excellent. I have included a quick photo I took of some tests I ran showing the metallics up close. I hope you can see it.

DRY TIME
These dry very quickly. On paper it is really fast. On canvas, it takes a little bit of time, but not much before you can put on another layer.

USE
You will need to use these. Once you get them, use them. They will most likely dry out pretty quickly and you won't get to have fun with them if you wait too long. This is the type of art tool you want to enjoy when you get it and not put it away for that project you will probably not get to anyway.

THE BOTTOM LINE
For models, artwork, and even rock paintings, these are decent acrylic marker pens. The paints are somewhat transparent in some colors, so plan accordingly

MY RATING
FIVE STARS. For what these are, they are really nice. I love the case and apprecaite how easy it is to see them, store them, and take them with me when I want to do a project. I can do it in a chair or at a table. I just have to remember to push to use them before they dry up at some point so I can enjoy them while they are still working.

This 24-piece acrylic paint pen kit is a blast--and at a little over $1 a pen, it gives you a lot of entertainment hours for your buck!The set comes in a beautifully decorated hardcover case, with the name "Ohuhu" (leaf in the 'O'), and drawings of leaves, flowers, stars, cactus, a cute gecko, peaceful dove, and other geometrics, designed to inspire, printed on the front in white. The back has Ohuhu's motto, "Draw. Feel. Empower." and a bunch of legal data printed on it. The zipper on the case moves very smoothly, and each pen has its own velcro loop to hold it secure in travel. This would make a perfect Plein Air sketch set, so light and easy to use.Inside, there is a multilingual instruction booklet and 3 swatch cards. 1 swatch card is filled out and has a white background, and there are also two blanks: one white and one black. I encourage you to fill both of these out, first, to prime your pens and get them ready to do an art, and second, so you can notice how the different background colors affect the perceived color of the pens. Even though you are using the exact same color on both cards, the final outcome looks VERY different. After that, you're ready to go!The colors of the paint are opaque, provided you let the bottom colors dry before adding more on top. This takes maybe a minute. You can also blend the colors just a bit by working two colors together quickly, but be careful that you don't foul and muddy your pen tips.Protip: if you've treated your item with gesso (highly recommended), you can blend, work, and even dilute the colors with a damp brush and a little water, allowing you to create watercolor-like effects or blend and smooth sharp lines. The gesso protects your item from the water and smooths the surface in order to accept the paint more readily. It's fairly cheap and available here on Amazon. Think of it as primer, except for art!These pens may not be as versatile as a full acrylic paint set, but neither are they as expensive or as messy. For a more advanced artist, these pens make a great color sketch set so you can get ideas down in the books quickly and conveniently, then you can use your full acrylic or oil paint set to make a full final copy. These paints are great for casual artists or smaller multimedia art projects such as rock painting or just adding a few quick touches to a knitting or sewing project. Not everybody wants or needs to bother with a full paint kit. These pens are also great for card-making and stencils. I'm sure there's a ton of other uses I've forgotten, or don't have the wit to imagine. 10/10, versatile, affordable, and FUN.

"30 Colors Waterproof Dual Tip Acrylic Paint Pens, Dot & Fine Tip" is a set of 30 markers with a dot tip on one side and a fine tip on the other. Unlike regular markers, these are filled with acrylic paint.

-------------
Pros:
* Using acrylic markers is faster and easier than using paint brushes.

* They don't need to be shaken and primed before use. You can just open the container and get started! (Unlike most markers that are filled with a substance that's thicker than ink.)

* The quality of the tips is adequate for multiple surfaces.

* The dot tip is surprisingly handy if you have trouble making perfect circles by hand, like most people do. XD

* The paint flows easily, so the markers move smoothly. That specifically makes them good for painting, writing, and detail work.

* The acrylic "ink" is easily layered, doesn't bleed (even on paper), and works well on multiple surfaces, which makes it a fantastic tool for craft projects.

* The acrylic is water-based, which makes it washable, so clean up is a breeze!

* The paint dries quickly.

* The pens -don't- dry out quickly.

* There's no strong smell.

-------------
Meh:
* The markers come in a range of pastel and medium colors with only a few dark and metallic colors. If that's what you're looking for, you're golden. If not, you won't buy these anyway, so it doesn't matter. :)

* The marker colors are named AND numbered, making finding replacements quick and easy. However, this is only true on the back of the box, NOT on the pens themselves, so you'll need to keep the list on the box / take a picture of it / whatever if you want that information.

* They suffer the same issues as using acrylic paints... because they ARE acrylic paints.

For example, the markers work on smooth surfaces like glass and plastic, but when you try to paint over a part that you've already painted, there's a chance that it will remove the paint on these surfaces instead of adding more (Sharpies and dry erase markers do this, too). And sometimes the lighter colors will be a little see-through, and might take multiple coats to fully cover a surface.

These are very common paint issues, but people sometimes seem to forget that acrylic markers are paint, not traditional markers, and as such, they act like paint. XD

-------------
Cons:
* None! At least, not yet. :)

-------------
With the quality, versatility, and variety of these paint markers, $30 for 80 markers ($0.38 each) is an absolute STEAL, even considering that you're getting less paint with each marker than is standard.

And even with taking the lack of replacement options into account, if given the choice, I would choose to order these again. The color variety is just too good to pass up. :)

I hope that this helps! :D

I am NOT an artist - I am a crafter and, therefore, my review is based on how I would use these paint markers. There’s a lot to like:
- There’s a nice variety of colors though some of are subtle variations
- The bullet (or dot) end is a nice bullet point, which will be good for mandala painting (for me, on river rocks)
- You can get a pretty fine line with the fine tip
- You don’t have to do a lot prep just to get started (e.g., pressing down nibs, waiting for paint to appear, etc.); simply uncap and go to town
- The caps click when closing so you know it’s firmly capped (some other markers have dried on me when I inadvertently did not put on the caps tight enough)
- While it’s waterproof on surfaces, it washes off clean from your hands.
- Good price point.

So why not 5 stars? Well…these might be minor to some, but for me, I was kind of “meh”:
- The colors are in no way labeled. Yes, you can see the color from the cap BUT, as I mentioned, a couple colors are very similar. I swatched all but one pen, but because there’s no number or name, I can’t figure out which one I missed.
- I do like a solid, clicking cap. However, there was an inconsistency - some caps were fine and easy to open; a few were on so tightly, it was a struggle to open. By the time I got one or two uncapped, I was grumpy.
- The coverage is okay, not super-duper. To get a good opaque coverage, you have to wait for one layer of color to dry then go over it. Not a big deal, but the white could be whiter. The silver and gold are nice but my other acrylic metallic markers are more shimmery/shiny. Again, not a bit deal.

Overall, for the number of pens, the quality of the color, and the price point, this is a good purchase - at least from a crafter’s perspective.

I buy and use a lot of art supplies. I painted the first rock partially white (base for a rocky mountain goat) and after 3 layers the paint is still thin. I painted the second rock black. After letting it dry layer by layer; I started painting flowers on the surface. Again adding 3 or 4 layers to deepen the colors of the petals, letting the paint dry in between. The added colors soaked up the black base paint making the flowers muddy. The end result was a "faded" look.
I painted on paper where it did better.
I would not recommend this paint set if you wanted to use it for anything other than paper - and do not mind the lack of vibrancy, and thinness.

This is a beautiful set of paint markers. My daughter's and I have been using them every day since they arrived. All 3 of us took turns doing the swatches. I didn't remove any stars for the numbering because the markers themselves are great.The colors are numbered - from 600's - 900's. 6 and 9 are the two worst possible numbers you can use for a numbering tangible items. It's so easy to conflate one for the other. Some of these pens caps had little dots on them (either above or below the 6 or 9?!) since no one knows if the dot indicates up or down/top or bottom, it's essentially just a useless decorative mark above or below a 6 or a 9 lol.About halfway into the color chart, I started to see a pattern and deduced that the colors seem to be more organized by their secondary tones/color temperatures as opposed to primary. I also realized that most are grouped into similar colors, so you can look in the same color family as the previous one for the next number. However, when a new undertone section starts, you won't know - and good luck finding the numbered pen you're looking for at that point haha.Aside from the numbering nightmare lol, these are perfect. Every single one worked flawlessly and had a great flow. The colors are vivid and there is pretty much every color you can think of. I did notice that a few tips were more flexible than others. I definitely prefer the firmer ones are they are easier to control for smaller designs - which is mostly what I do.  This set also includes extra tips - which is appreciated.If your planning to buy this set of 240 paint pens, keep an eye on the price. When I acquired this, it was selling for close to $150. At the time of this review, it's selling for $118. If you break it down, it's like 50¢ per marker. Which is pretty reasonable compared to Posca. I think this set would make an awesome gift for anyone who loves art. My teenage daughter's and I have been painting rocks with these and they work beautifully for it. But there are so many applications for these besides just rocks. We are very happy with them and although the color swatching was a bit maddening, I really did enjoy the challenge of it.
